01
Lasers, recycling & automation

An old solar cell still has something to give.

Published work

A worn-out solar cell is still full of useful material. The question that got me interested was simple: could a laser help us get that material back, without destroying everything around it?

I developed ways to recover silver from silicon and CIGS solar cells, either as larger pieces or as tiny particles. That meant choosing a laser, changing the processing conditions, and looking closely at what came off—and what was left behind. I also worked on removing the polymer backsheet from a module while keeping its glass and silicon intact.

Then came a very practical problem: broken cells don’t arrive in neat, identical shapes. I used image segmentation and Python to find the metal contacts in a picture and turn them into paths the laser could follow. My childhood interest in making things move more or less found its natural habitat.

For the curious (and the technically curious)Silver recovery + deep-learning automation · 2025Silver recovery from CIGS · 2025Backsheet removal through glass · 2026Selective silver debonding · 2024
What stayed with me

Getting a material off is only half the job. Knowing what you recovered, what you damaged, and whether you can repeat it is the other half.

02
Single-crystal growth & battery materials

Before testing a material, sometimes you have to grow it.

Published work

Working with materials at IIT Delhi took me a step further back in the story: how do you make the sample you want to study in the first place?

My work involved single-crystal growth, pulsed laser deposition, vacuum systems, and measurements of structure and electronic properties. It was hands-on work: prepare a sample, check what actually formed, and work out which part of the process needs another try.

I’m also a co-author on a study of MoSeTe as a possible anode for sodium-ion batteries. Sodium is abundant, which makes the search for suitable battery materials especially interesting. The study looked at both the material’s structure and how it behaved during charging and discharging.

For the curious (and the technically curious)MoSeTe for sodium-ion batteries · 2022
What stayed with me

A good first result is an invitation to keep testing. How a material behaves over repeated cycles matters just as much.

03
Transparent conducting oxide films

A very thin film. Quite a lot to figure out.

Published work

Some materials need to let light through and carry electricity at the same time. That combination led me into transparent conducting oxide films during my MSc at IIT Ropar.

I made antimony-doped tin oxide films using thermal evaporation followed by controlled oxidation. Then I checked their crystal structure, how much light passed through, and how easily current flowed.

The interesting part was connecting those measurements back to how the film had been made. A layer that looks unremarkable on a piece of glass can have a very different story once you measure it.

For the curious (and the technically curious)Sb-doped SnO₂ thin films · 2019
What stayed with me

Making the film and measuring the film belong in the same conversation. Otherwise, it is very easy to optimize the wrong thing.

04
Low-light imaging & scientific computing

What can a camera see when there’s barely any light?

Ongoing research

In dim light, a camera has very little signal to work with. Noise starts to compete with the scene itself. I’m interested in understanding that noise and how we evaluate attempts to recover the image.

My work brings together RAW image analysis, statistical noise modeling, Python, and image-restoration evaluation. I work with the measurements behind an image as well as the image we eventually look at.

This is another place where my physics and programming interests meet. It is also a useful reminder that a prettier picture and a more faithful measurement are different questions.

What stayed with me

Start by understanding the noise. Then ask whether an apparent improvement survives a careful, controlled comparison.

Still in the notebook

Two more stories are on their way.

Some work needs a little more time before it can leave the lab.

Unpublished work

A closer look at solar cells.

TEM–CL photovoltaics. I analyze light emitted under an electron beam alongside microscopy images of TiOₓ/Al₂O₃/Si contacts. The question is which features come from the material, and which come from the way we process the measurements.

I test spectral reconstruction and interference corrections to separate repeatable signals from processing artifacts. The manuscript is in preparation; the lesson so far is to question the processing as carefully as the experiment.

Under review

Listening to a material in more than one way.

Multimodal spectroscopy. I developed a platform that measures Raman, fluorescence, and LIBS signals using a single 355 nm pulsed laser, shared optics, fiber-coupled spectroscopy, and motorized positioning. That lets us ask different questions about the same spot on a mineral.

The manuscript on planetary minerals is under review at IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Quantum Electronics. Building the system taught me how much useful science depends on getting the optics and motion to work together.
